knowledge: Discovery starts with everyone the system touches: end users, their managers, data owners, security, legal and compliance, operations and the executive sponsor. A missing stakeholder usually surfaces later as a blocking constraint.
Capture the current process and its baseline metrics (time per task, error rate, volume, cost per task) before designing anything. Without a baseline, no one can prove the solution helped.
Success criteria should be specific, measurable, achievable and relevant, and agreed with the business owner up front. They cover quality, latency, cost and safety, not only accuracy.
Data questions decide feasibility: where the data lives, who owns it, how fresh and complete it is, how permissions are represented, and what regulated data (PHI, PII) it contains.
Constraints are requirements too: deployment and authorization rules, data residency, retention, required human sign-off, deadlines and budget per task.

A short prototype on representative real data (handled under the approved controls) is the cheapest feasibility check. Demos on synthetic or hand-picked examples overstate what production will achieve.
skills: Build a stakeholder map and run interviews or workshops with each group, including the people who do the work today.
Turn a vague goal ("make clinicians faster") into measurable success criteria with a baseline, a target and a measurement method.
Profile the real data early: sample it, check quality and freshness, and identify who must approve its use.
Run a time-boxed prototype on real data and score it against the draft success criteria before committing to scope and dates.
Record risks (data gaps, regulatory limits, LLM failure modes) with owners and mitigations in the discovery output.
examLens: Asked for the best first step in a new engagement, pick the answer that widens discovery to missing stakeholders or establishes a baseline, not one that starts building.
Prefer measurable success criteria agreed with the business owner over subjective goals or criteria the architect sets alone.
When feasibility is uncertain, prefer a prototype on representative real data over more slideware or a full build.
If an executive target depends on data that is late, incomplete or restricted, surface it during discovery rather than designing around it silently.
traps: Discovery limited to IT and the sponsor, skipping end users, data owners, legal or security.
Jumping to model or vendor selection before the problem, data and success criteria are understood.
Treating a polished demo on synthetic or cherry-picked data as proof of feasibility.
Accepting "high accuracy" or "faster" as success criteria with no baseline or measurement method.

knowledge: Tailor the message to the audience. Executives need the outcome, risk, cost, timeline and the decision being asked of them; engineers need components, interfaces and design details; legal and security need data flows, controls and accountability.

An architecture decision record (ADR) captures the context, the options considered, the decision, the trade-offs accepted and the consequences, so the reasoning survives after the meeting and the people.
Quantify trade-offs with evidence from your own evaluations (quality on the eval set, latency percentiles, cost per task) rather than intuition or vendor claims.
Be candid about LLM limitations: outputs are non-deterministic, models can hallucinate, and no design guarantees zero errors. Explain the measured error rate and the mitigations instead.
Present options with a recommendation. A decision-maker should see what each option costs and risks, and what would make you revisit the choice.
skills: Write an executive one-pager and a separate engineering design document from the same decision.
Write ADRs that list rejected options and why, with eval results attached.
Translate metrics into business terms (analyst hours saved, clinician minutes per note, error rate per thousand cases).
Answer "will it ever be wrong?" honestly with measured error rates, mitigations and residual risk.
Frame contested decisions (security versus productivity) as explicit options with risks, a recommendation and revisit criteria.
examLens: For executives, pick the answer framed around outcome, risk, cost and timeline with a clear ask, not the most technically detailed one.
For a contested or consequential design choice, prefer an ADR or written decision with options considered and evidence over a verbal agreement.
Prefer answers backed by your eval results over claims about model capability or vendor benchmarks.
Reject any answer that promises zero hallucinations, identical outputs every time or guaranteed fairness.
traps: One deck for every audience, usually too technical for executives and too vague for engineers.
Overpromising accuracy or determinism to win approval.
Recording only the chosen option, so nobody later knows why the alternatives were rejected.
Justifying a choice with a public benchmark instead of results on the client's own data.

knowledge: SLAs and SLOs must be measurable: latency percentiles, availability, and quality measured on an agreed eval set or sampled production review, each with a measurement method and owner.
LLM quality is statistical. Because outputs are non-deterministic, quality targets are rates over a defined test set or sample, never a promise about every single response.
The system depends on upstream services, including the model provider. Availability commitments should name those dependencies and define degraded-mode behaviour and incident communication.
Pilots need structured feedback channels inside the workflow (ratings, reason codes, edits captured), triaged regularly, with recurring issues turned into eval cases.
Scope creep is managed through the agreed success criteria and a change process: new requests are assessed for impact on quality, cost and deadlines, then scheduled or explicitly traded off.
Expectations are reset with evidence: pre-agreed thresholds and pause criteria let one anecdote be weighed against measured rates.
skills: Turn "always accurate and instant" into SLOs with targets, percentiles, test sets and measurement windows.
Write availability terms that cover provider dependencies, fallbacks and degraded modes.
Design in-workflow feedback capture and a regular triage loop that feeds the eval suite.
Run new feature requests through a change process that shows their effect on agreed targets.
Agree pause and rollback criteria before a pilot starts.
examLens: Prefer measurable SLOs defined over an eval set or sample over absolute promises such as 100% accuracy or identical outputs.
When feedback is informal or anecdotal, pick the answer that structures capture and links it to evals before changing prompts.
For a mid-pilot request, pick the change-control answer that assesses impact against agreed criteria, not silent acceptance or flat refusal.
When a stakeholder reacts to one bad case, investigate it, then weigh it against measured rates and pre-agreed thresholds.
traps: Accepting an SLA that guarantees perfect accuracy or deterministic outputs.
Committing to availability without accounting for the model provider and other upstream dependencies.
Collecting feedback in hallway conversations and changing prompts on the loudest complaint.
Measuring only system metrics (on-time delivery) and missing whether users act on the output.

knowledge: Core architecture documentation: context and component diagrams, data flow diagrams showing where sensitive data travels, is logged and is retained, and the trust boundaries between components.
Prompts, tool definitions and model choices are versioned artifacts. Keep them in source control with a change log and link each version to its eval results.
The eval suite is a living specification: test cases, graders and pass thresholds define what "working" means and guard every later change.
Runbooks cover known failure modes and operational tasks: provider errors, stale indexes, quality drift alerts, rollback and escalation contacts.
Guardrails need written rationale (the risk mitigated, the owner, the exception process), or teams remove them as friction.

A handoff package gives the receiving team what they need to own the system: architecture and data flows, versioned prompts and configs, the eval suite, runbooks, monitoring dashboards and open risks.
skills: Draw data flow diagrams that security and compliance reviewers can approve.
Set up prompt and configuration versioning with an eval gate before promotion.
Write runbooks keyed to observable symptoms and alerts.
Document each guardrail with its rationale, owner and exception route next to the configuration.
Give implementation teams interface contracts, output schemas and eval cases rather than prose descriptions.
examLens: For a security or compliance review, pick the data flow and trust-boundary artifact over general architecture prose.
For untracked prompt changes that broke quality, pick versioning plus an eval gate before release.
For a handoff, prefer artifacts the receiving team can operate and test with (eval suite, runbooks, configs) over meeting notes or slide decks.
When teams keep bypassing a control, pick documenting its rationale and exception process before tightening enforcement alone.
traps: Editing prompts directly in production with no version history or eval run.
Handing over slide decks and transcripts instead of operable artifacts.
Documenting what a guardrail does but not why it exists.
Treating the eval suite as a one-off launch test instead of a living spec.

knowledge: A Claude solution moves through discovery, design, build and pilot, handoff, monitoring and iteration. Each phase has exit criteria agreed with stakeholders.
Moving from pilot to wide rollout should depend on evidence: agreed quality, safety and fairness thresholds met, operating team named and trained, monitoring in place.
After handoff, a named owner is accountable for monitoring, the eval suite, incident response and the backlog. Without one, quality drift goes unnoticed.
Model upgrades and deprecations are planned events: run the existing eval suite on the new model, compare results, roll out in stages and migrate before the retirement date.
Iteration uses production evidence (telemetry, feedback, failure cases) compared against the discovery baseline, and every change is re-evaluated before release.
Retiring a data source, tool or the system itself also needs planning: inventory dependencies, test the replacement, and tell users what will change and when.
skills: Define exit criteria for each phase, especially pilot to rollout.
Plan staged rollouts with representative pilot groups and comparison against the baseline.
Assign post-handoff ownership and the monitoring and alert thresholds that owner acts on.
Run model migration as an eval-gated change with rollback.
Plan deprecations of models, tools and data sources with dependency inventories and user communication.
examLens: For a new model version or deprecation notice, pick re-running the eval suite and staged migration, not switching on announcement or waiting until retirement.
For pilot to rollout, pick evidence-based exit criteria plus operational readiness, not enthusiasm or feature completeness.
For silent degradation after handoff, the root cause is usually missing ownership and monitoring, not the model.
Prefer a representative pilot with a baseline comparison over a big-bang rollout.
traps: Treating handoff as the end of the project, with no owner for monitoring or evals.
Adopting a newer model because it is newer, without running the eval suite.
Rolling out to everyone at once with no pilot or comparison group.
Gating rollout on stakeholder satisfaction or on finishing every requested feature.
